analysis.title: Artificial Intelligence: Managing Concentration Risk
key_insights: AI concentration is rising across the economy and in portfolios. The report argues investors should manage it rather than abandon AI exposure, since AI has delivered strong returns and economy-wide productivity potential.

AI is unfolding in three overlapping stages: transformative innovation (semiconductors the main beneficiaries), infrastructure buildout (hyperscalers, neoclouds, data centers, utilities), and diffusion across the broader economy, which the authors call potentially the most economically consequential.

US AI infrastructure capex could top US$9 trillion over the next six years, equal to 3.2% of annual US GDP (NBER working paper). The buildout is a significant contributor to, and a risk for, US real GDP growth in the second half of the decade.

Adoption is rising quickly: 78% of businesses in seven countries used AI as of mid-2026, up from 69% six months earlier. Average US AI spend is US$2,000 per employee, and 2% of US and UK firms account for 50% of AI spending.

Measured productivity gains among adopters are modest: 0.2% average annual rate in sales per employee, with respondents expecting 0.6% over the next three years. The authors cite steam, rail, electricity and the internet as precedents for slow diffusion.

Hyperscalers are about 17.8% of S&P 500 market cap and other AI enablers and adopters another 28.1%, together nearly 46%. MSCI's AI Value Chain puts AI-associated companies at about US$21.8 trillion, or 19% of global equity market cap.

TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix are about 30% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index and 36% of MSCI EM Asia, so moving from US tech to Asian semiconductors only swaps one part of the AI ecosystem for another.

AI concentration extends to credit: about US$330 billion of AI-related bonds issued in 1H 2026, roughly 16% of outstanding investment-grade corporate debt. About US$32 billion of AI high-yield issuance in 1H 2026 was roughly 40% of net new high-yield issuance but only about 4% of the outstanding high-yield market.

In private markets, AI-related companies are about a quarter of direct lending and over 15% of private equity investments. Investors can hold overlapping AI exposure across public equity, IG, HY, private equity, private credit and infrastructure.

Capex is reducing free cash flow even at the most profitable players, which pushes them toward borrowing. Credit markets are differentiating: highly leveraged neoclouds face sharply higher financing costs and more creditworthy AI borrowers have seen modest spread widening.

A central question is whether AI returns will keep exceeding the cost of capital, given higher risk premiums and rising global real rates. Aggregate AI success does not guarantee returns for each financier or each form of exposure.

Diversification depends on the scenario. An inflation surge (as in 2022) hurts stocks and bonds together. Rising real yields from faster productivity growth can coexist with strong equities, but real yields rising on fiscal crowding-out could hurt both. A growth or AI-returns disappointment would restore the hedging value of high-quality government and non-AI corporate bonds.

Mitigation options: shift from cap-weighted passive to equal-weight, select downstream AI adopters, tilt credit toward balance-sheet strength and manageable refinancing, add select local-currency EM debt (e.g. Latin America), use alternative risk premia and hedge funds, and apply a total portfolio approach that covers liquidity and overlapping issuers and counterparties.

A 'barbell' of AI exposure plus core high-quality fixed income is proposed, with Treasuries and similar assets acting as ballast in an AI-driven cyclical slowdown. They do not diversify inflation risk.

sector_views.rationale: Keep AI exposure for returns and productivity upside but manage concentration through equal-weight, downstream adopters and diversifiers.
Higher yields give income, and Treasuries should act as ballast in an AI-driven slowdown. They do not hedge an inflation shock.
Select markets such as Latin America offer high real yields tied to fundamentals not closely linked to AI.

trade_ideas.description: Barbell: hold AI equity exposure alongside high-quality core fixed income (Treasuries, higher-quality sovereigns, MBS, non-AI investment-grade credit)
trade_ideas.rationale: Government and non-AI IG bonds are likely to act as ballast in an AI-induced cyclical slowdown.
trade_ideas.risk: Bonds do not diversify inflation risk, and an inflation surge can hit stocks and bonds together.

trade_ideas.description: Shift passive cap-weighted equity to equal-weight strategies to reduce AI concentration
trade_ideas.rationale: Passive index holdings have become more concentrated in AI.

trade_ideas.description: Add alternative risk premia and hedge fund strategies as non-directional diversifiers
trade_ideas.rationale: Returns derive from spreads and manager skill that are not linked to broad stock and bond markets.

risk_factors: Higher financing costs or other factors slowing the AI buildout would slow macro growth.
Semiconductor revenues depend on hyperscaler capex, data-center profitability on computing demand, and computing demand on AI applications generating enough value downstream.
Rising real rates driven by fiscal crowding-out could hurt both stocks and bonds.
An inflation surge, as in 2022, can lower equity and bond prices together.
Highly leveraged neoclouds face higher financing costs and refinancing risk.
Rising use of less-liquid private assets raises liquidity risk.

vol_and_positioning: Hyperscalers and AI-adjacent names are about 46% of S&P 500 market cap, and passive index holders have seen AI concentration rise. Equal-weight strategies are proposed to reduce it.

Over three years hyperscalers outperformed both the cap-weighted and equal-weighted S&P 500 with higher volatility. The hyperscaler equal-weighted index stood at 186 versus 128 for the S&P 500 equal-weighted index (rebased to 100 on June 9, 2023, as of Oct 30, 2026).
Overlapping AI exposure across public and private assets is the main portfolio risk. A total portfolio approach is suggested to detect common issuers, counterparties and technologies.

tension_points.bull_case: Concentration reflects exceptional performance, and hyperscalers outperformed the cap-weighted and equal-weighted S&P 500 over three years. Cutting exposure indiscriminately would sacrifice returns from a major innovation.
tension_points.bear_case: Companies across different industries depend on the same drivers (hyperscaler capex, computing demand, downstream AI value), and borrowing to fund capex is raising financing costs and risk premiums.
tension_points.what_invalidates: AI returns falling below the cost of capital, or financing costs slowing the buildout, would undermine the bull case.

theme_stances.key_argument: Investors should manage AI concentration through diversification and hedging rather than abandon AI exposure.
Capex is cutting free cash flow and pushing AI firms to borrow, so leveraged neoclouds face sharply higher financing costs.
theme_stances.evidence: Highly leveraged neocloud companies have experienced sharp increases in financing costs
